title: Convolutional networks, LeCun, cheque reading by 1998
story:
Treat an image as a list of pixels and feed it to a fully connected layer, and you have thrown away two facts about images before learning begins.

The first is that nearby pixels are related and distant ones mostly are not. A fully connected layer has no notion of adjacency at all — shuffle the pixels consistently and it learns exactly as well, which tells you it was never using the spatial arrangement.

The second is that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears. An edge in the corner and an edge in the centre are the same kind of thing, but a fully connected layer has separate parameters for every position, so it must learn the same pattern independently in each place and needs examples of it in each place to do so.

A convolutional layer builds both facts in. It applies the same small set of weights across every position of the image, so each unit looks only at a local neighbourhood, and the weights are shared across all positions.

Follow what those two choices buy, because they are the entire argument. Locality means each unit has few inputs regardless of how large the image is. Sharing means one pattern is learned once and available everywhere — so the parameter count depends on the size of the detector and the number of detectors, and not on the size of the image. A larger image costs more computation and no more parameters. And because a detector learned from examples in one part of the image applies to all parts, the effective number of training examples for that detector is multiplied by the number of positions.

LeCun, Bottou, Bengio and Haffner published Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition in the Proceedings of the IEEE in November 1998, describing convolutional networks trained by gradient descent and applied to handwritten document recognition, including systems deployed commercially — and arguing that a network can learn its own features from pixels rather than having them designed by hand.

That last argument is the part worth noticing, because it is what the field later confirmed at scale. The claim was not only that this architecture works. It was that hand-designed feature extraction, then the standard practice, could be replaced by learning.

The deployment matters for the same reason, and deserves care with the numbers. The architecture's descendants went into commercial cheque-reading systems, with one manufacturer fielding them from 1996, and a widely repeated retrospective estimate puts the system at about 20 million cheques a day around 2001 — roughly a tenth of those in the United States. That percentage is an estimate made afterwards rather than an audited statistic or a figure from the paper, and different retellings give different values, so it is worth quoting with the hedge attached.

The point survives the imprecision, and it is worth stating plainly because the popular history of this field usually skips it. This was not a promising laboratory result waiting for its moment. It was in production, at national scale, on money, more than a decade before the approach was widely considered viable. What was missing afterwards was never a demonstration that it worked.

The cost of the design is that its assumptions are not optional. A convolutional layer assumes locality and assumes that position does not change meaning, and there is no setting that turns those off. Where they do not hold — data with no spatial structure, or where absolute position carries meaning — the architecture is not merely unhelpful but actively wrong, encoding a prior that the data contradicts. Choosing it is a claim about the data, which is the general form of what an architecture is.

problem.move: Build the known structure in rather than hoping it is learned: apply the same small detector across all positions so patterns learned anywhere apply everywhere. Then check that the assumptions hold, because they are not optional and cannot be switched off.
problem.invariant: Sharing weights across positions makes the parameter count depend on the detector and not the input size, and multiplies the effective training examples for each detector by the number of positions it is applied at.
problem.breaks: The assumptions are the architecture. Where locality fails or absolute position carries meaning, the design is not merely unhelpful but encodes a prior the data contradicts — and no setting disables it, so choosing this architecture is a claim about the data.

cost.time: the same detector is evaluated at every position, so computation grows with input size even though parameters do not
cost.space: activations at every position must be held, which is where the memory goes
cost.beats: a fully connected layer, which assumes nothing and needs a parameter per position and examples in every position, and hand-designed feature extraction, which encodes what you already know and cannot find what you do not

worked.reasoning:
It assumes two things: that nearby inputs are related and distant ones mostly are not, and that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears.

It is worth seeing what is discarded without them. problem.practice: Take an image model and count its parameters, then double the input resolution and count again. The number that changes is the computation, not the parameters — and seeing that once explains why the design exists.

beats.broke: Treating an image as an unstructured list discards the facts that nearby pixels are related and that a pattern means the same thing anywhere, so the model must learn both from scratch and needs examples in every position.
beats.fix: Apply the same small detector across every position, so each unit sees a local neighbourhood and what is learned in one place is available everywhere.
beats.cost: The assumptions are the architecture and cannot be switched off, so data where locality fails or absolute position matters is served by a prior it contradicts.

interview.q: What does a convolutional layer assume, and what do those assumptions buy?
interview.trap: Answering only that it reduces parameters. The larger consequence is that a detector learned from examples in one region applies everywhere, which multiplies the effective training data for it — that is why these models need less data than their parameter count suggests.
interview.answer:
It assumes nearby inputs are related and distant ones mostly are not, and that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears.

What that replaces is worth stating. Sharing means the parameter count depends on detector size and count rather than input size, so a larger image costs more computation and no more parameters. And — the one usually left out and the most practically important — a detector learned from examples in one region applies to all regions, so its effective training data is multiplied by the number of positions, which is why these models need less data than their parameter count suggests.

The 1998 paper describes exactly this applied to handwritten document recognition including commercially deployed systems, and its more radical claim was that a network can learn its own features from pixels rather than having them designed by hand — hand-designed extraction being the standard practice then.

On deployment I would hedge deliberately: descendants went into commercial cheque readers from 1996, and a widely repeated retrospective estimate puts it near 20 million cheques a day around 2001, roughly a tenth of those in the United States. That percentage is an estimate made afterwards rather than an audited figure or one from the paper, and retellings differ. The point survives the imprecision — this was in production at national scale, on money, more than a decade before the approach was widely considered viable, so what was missing afterwards was never a demonstration that it worked.

The cost is the general lesson: the assumptions are not optional. Where locality fails or absolute position carries meaning, the architecture encodes a prior the data contradicts and no setting turns it off. Choosing an architecture is making a claim about the data.
